flashcards.q: What is the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
flashcards.a: A behavioral pattern that passes a request along a chain of handlers; each handler either processes the request or forwards it to the next.

flashcards.q: What are the three participants in the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
flashcards.a: 1) Handler (abstract: setNext, handle), 2) ConcreteHandler (canHandle, process, or forward), 3) Client (sends request to first handler).

flashcards.q: How does Chain of Responsibility decouple sender and receiver?
flashcards.a: The sender only sends to the first handler; it doesn't know which handler (if any) will process the request.

flashcards.q: When should you use the Chain of Responsibility pattern?
flashcards.a: When multiple objects can handle a request and you don't want the sender to know which, or when building a pipeline (middleware, validation, logging).

flashcards.q: How does Chain of Responsibility differ from Decorator?
flashcards.a: Decorator wraps one object and always forwards. Chain handlers may stop (not forward); chain is a linked list of handlers, not a wrapper stack.

flashcards.q: What is a common risk if no handler in the chain handles the request?
flashcards.a: The request falls through with no processing; use a default/final handler at the end so every request is handled.

flashcards.q: Name 3 common uses for Chain of Responsibility.
flashcards.a: Middleware (auth, logging, validation), event handling (pass until handled), support escalation (level 1 → 2 → 3).
Often the handler that was set (or the next handler) to allow fluent chain building: h1.setNext(h2).setNext(h3).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between 'first handler wins' and 'all handlers run'?
flashcards.a: First wins: handler processes and stops. All run: each handler does something and passes on (e.g. logging pipeline).

flashcards.q: How does Chain of Responsibility relate to middleware?
flashcards.a: Middleware stacks (e.g. in web frameworks) are often implemented as a chain of responsibility: each middleware can respond or call next().
Order often determines behavior (e.g. auth before business logic, logging first); document or make order explicit in configuration.

flashcards.q: When is Chain of Responsibility overkill?
flashcards.a: When exactly one handler should process each request and you know which one; direct call is simpler.

flashcards.q: What does each ConcreteHandler do in handle()?
flashcards.a: It checks if it can handle the request (canHandle); if yes, processes and returns; if no, forwards to next.handle(request).

flashcards.q: How can the chain be built?
flashcards.a: At construction (e.g. new Handler1().setNext(new Handler2())) or at runtime from config; client only needs reference to the first handler.
